definition: Unicode assigns a code point, a number, to almost every written character. Stored text is those numbers encoded as bytes, most often with UTF-8. A character a person sees is not always one code point, and a code point is not always one byte.
details: UTF-8 uses one byte for ASCII and up to four bytes for other characters. Slicing a string by bytes can cut a character in half.
Comparing text sometimes requires a normalized form, because one character can be encoded as one code point or as a base plus a combining mark.
examples: A name containing an accented letter
An emoji stored as more than one code point
